title: The hypertrophy series: using supersets to bridge volume gaps
summary: NH presents supersets mainly as a tool for filling rest time with tonnage and paying off the tonnage debt of lagging small muscles. Everything except opening strength work can be supersetted, but you should avoid pre-fatiguing stabilizers like the abs and build volume and frequency patiently before adding load.
claims: Supersets compress training by filling time that would otherwise be spent resting
Most people who are resting should be working; three-minute rests after curls are a waste of time
Supersets should first be seen as a way to bridge volume gaps, rather than as an intensity technique
Lagging body parts are usually small muscles that grow from isolation, which people neglected, building up a tonnage debt that takes years to pay off
Catch up lagging muscles by hitting them with frequent, repeated, low-intensity sets placed as supersets
Never superset the strength work that opens a session; everything after it can be supersetted
His program is entirely supersets, some of them giant sets of up to five exercises, which lets him pile up tonnage without hurting recovery or risking injury
Superset exercises with no cardio cost, no setup time and little tendon stress: calves, medial and lateral triceps heads, biceps, traps, rear delts and to some extent abs
Don't superset muscles that stabilise compound lifts, like the abs, right before a compound that needs core rigidity
A newly isolated muscle is weak and burns out within two or three sets, so start slowly; patience is the price of past neglect
Untrained calves tire quickly and the feet and ankles hurt at first; build up their capacity slowly
Progress superset volume gradually: add two isolation sets to a superset, then three or four, then spread them to other days until weekly frequency is maxed, and only then add weight
Adding weight while keeping sets constant turns the work into strength work and won't pay off the tonnage debt
